final_recommendation: The room converged on a surgical labor-only amendment with binding enforcement mechanisms (independent inspectors, 30-day month notice with 48-hour facility selection, automatic 90-day tariff snapback, monthly wage reporting). The Wednesday 6 AM draft locks all language—Spanish 'notificarán' for Mexico, explicit carve-out preserving Canada's dairy/tariff concessions—and business commits to Thursday swing-district outreach with fourteen named Republicans. Ratification prospects rose from 40 to 62 as all parties confirmed final text with no pending rewrites.
minority_objections: Canada initially hesitated on pre-committing to defend 30-day notice language without full domestic vetting (R3)
Mexico resisted unannounced facility access as sovereignty infringement, demanding announced schedules before accepting 48-hour compromise (R2)
key_conflicts: Congress vs. Mexico on unannounced inspections: Democrats demanded surprise access; Mexico called it 'occupation' and required 30-day month notice with 48-hour site selection (R2-R3)
Labor union vs. Mexico on veto rights: union demanded zero deferral/objection power; Mexico needed 'notificación' not 'consulta' to avoid domestic sovereignty backlash (R4-R5)
Congress vs. business on Republican whip count: Democrats demanded named swing-district Republicans before counting votes; business delivered fourteen names conditional on locked text (R4-R5)
key_concessions: Mexico accepted independent inspectors with 30-day month notice + 48-hour facility selection, abandoning demand for fully announced schedules (R3)
Congress accepted 30-day month notice framework instead of pure surprise inspections, gaining 48-hour unpredictability window (R3)
Canada accepted labor amendment reopening in exchange for explicit carve-out locking dairy/tariff concessions (R2-R4)
Business committed Thursday board-chair outreach to fourteen swing-district Republicans, conditional on final text (R5-R6)
red_lines: Labor union: independent inspectors with unannounced access, automatic snapback with zero deferral, monthly wage reporting—'we walk if they're not in writing' (R2)
Mexico: 'notificación' not 'consulta' in Spanish text; no veto interpretation or semantic drift post-ratification (R5-R6)
Canada: labor-only amendment with explicit lock on dairy/tariff concessions; 'we're done' if U.S. tries creative reopening (R4, R6)
Congress: binding enforcement mechanisms visible in Wednesday draft or 'this doesn't move'; Republican votes contingent on locked text (R1, R5)
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Enforcement implementation risk: no discussion of inspector training, binational board composition, or dispute resolution if Mexico challenges findings post-inspection
Domestic political backlash in Mexico: room focused on sovereignty framing ('notificación') but did not model how Mexican public/opposition parties react to foreign inspectors on the ground
Republican defection risk post-Thursday: business delivered fourteen names but no mechanism to hold them accountable if labor enforcement becomes politically toxic in their districts
Agreement stability beyond ratification: no discussion of what happens if Mexico misses wage benchmarks and snapback triggers—does the deal survive the first enforcement action?
downstream_risk_variables: Republican vote stability: fourteen swing-district Republicans committed conditional on locked text, but no binding mechanism if they defect post-Thursday outreach
Mexico's domestic ratification: room locked Spanish 'notificación' language but did not model whether Mexican legislature accepts foreign inspectors as sovereignty-compatible
Enforcement trigger credibility: automatic 90-day snapback sounds binding, but no discussion of political will to actually impose tariffs if Mexico misses benchmarks
Canada's Parliament defense: Canada confirmed support for labor-only amendment but flagged uncertainty on defending 30-day notice framework domestically (R3)
uncertainty_notes: The room achieved textual convergence (locked Wednesday draft, Spanish phrasing, carve-out language) but left three critical uncertainties unresolved: (1) whether the fourteen Republicans actually vote yes after Thursday calls or defect under constituent pressure; (2) whether Mexico's domestic ratification process accepts the inspector framework despite sovereignty concerns; (3) whether the automatic snapback mechanism survives first contact with political reality if Mexico misses wage benchmarks and U.S. faces pressure to defer enforcement.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Drove every round: Congress opened with 'this deal doesn't pass the House as written' (R1), demanded Republican whip count before counting votes (R3-R5), and made Thursday outreach contingent on locked text. Ratification prospects rose from 40→62 as room resolved enforcement language.
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Central driver: labor union set three non-negotiables (independent inspectors, unannounced access, automatic snapback) in R2, demanded 'notificación' not 'consulta' in R4-R5, and threatened to walk endorsement if interpretation shifted (R6). Shaped entire amendment framework.
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Medium: business committed board-chair outreach and delivered fourteen Republican names (R4-R5), but conditioned support on locked text and did not drive the room's direction—followed Congress/labor demands rather than setting agenda.
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Medium: Canada demanded explicit carve-out locking dairy/tariff concessions (R2, R4, R6) and flagged uncertainty on defending 30-day notice domestically (R3), but did not block progress—accepted labor amendment once carve-out was embedded.
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Drove R2-R5: Mexico called unannounced inspections 'occupation' (R2), demanded 'notificación' not 'consulta' to avoid veto-right interpretation (R4-R5), and required on-record commitment that interpretation wouldn't drift (R6). Shaped 30-day/48-hour compromise.
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Medium: media actor set Wednesday deadline for locked text (R1-R2), warned 'stalled again' narrative would kill momentum (R3-R6), and forced trade lawyer to confirm final draft status (R6)—but did not drive substantive enforcement design.
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Medium: room treated amendment as necessary for ratification (Congress: 'doesn't pass as written'), but focused on locking current text rather than modeling post-ratification enforcement stability or snapback-trigger scenarios.
